appraisal_events.evidence: As "fils Swann" he receives the bourgeoisie's amiability, which "ne se sépare jamais de la considération"; if he were struck down at home his valet would naturally run for "le duc de Chartres, le prince de Reuss, le duc de Luxembourg, et le baron de Charlus"; and he can turn back to "un monde pour qui il était l'homme exquis par excellence, qu'on faisait tout pour attirer, qu'on se désolait de ne pas voir".
appraisal_events.explanation: The narration establishes Swann's standing in both the world and the solid bourgeoisie as secure, sought-after, and hereditary — a position wholly independent of the one he occupies with Odette.

appraisal_events.evidence: Where he must excuse himself to society for not calling, "c'était de lui en faire qu'il cherchait à s'excuser auprès d'Odette"; he pays for the visits ("si c'était assez de lui envoyer quatre mille francs") and invents pretexts, begging Charlus to fetch her; she pleads propriety, says "qu'il voulait afficher leur liaison, qu'il la traitait comme une fille", keeps him only until a better offer comes; he ends by sobbing alone at night — "je deviens névropathe" — and welcoming the thought of a fatal tumour.
appraisal_events.explanation: The same man the world courts must buy, excuse and stage-manage each meeting with a woman who refuses to be seen with him; the narrator's reversal of the two registers makes the abasement, and the exhaustion it ends in, the passage's dominant movement.

appraisal_events.evidence: After Adolphe advises Swann to stay away and Odette to let him meet her anywhere, Odette tells Swann "qu'elle venait d'avoir une déception en voyant que mon oncle était pareil à tous les hommes : il venait d'essayer de la prendre de force"; Swann refuses his hand at their next meeting.
appraisal_events.explanation: Odette's accusation, delivered just after the uncle's advice went against her, destroys a long friendship and costs Swann his one route to the truth about Nice; the narration neither confirms nor denies the charge.

appraisal_events.evidence: He gathers that "cette légèreté des mœurs d'Odette… était assez connue", that at Bade and Nice "elle avait eu une sorte de notoriété galante", that she is "peut-être trop connue des fêtards, des hommes à femmes"; against this he tells himself "Ces réputations-là, même vraies, sont faites avec les idées des autres".
appraisal_events.explanation: Society's reported voice attaches a compromised past to Odette, but the passage keeps its truth undecidable and lets Swann's counter-argument stand beside it.

status_effects.explanation: Inside the passage's world he is the exquisite man everyone works to attract, with princes and dukes as his natural intimates and the bourgeoisie's considered regard behind him.
He pays, apologizes, and waits on her convenience; the suffering runs to nightly sobbing and a wish for death to end the labour of it.
She bars him from every space where she can be seen — theatre, private view, charity fête — and will not let him wait in her house, so he is held outside a door he once had free.
She grants or withholds each meeting at the last minute, leaves the moment a better invitation comes, and turns his sadness into a grievance against him.
He is reported to have assaulted Odette and is cut by an old friend who will no longer take his hand.
The rumour of a galante notoriety at Nice and Bade lowers how she is spoken of, though the passage never settles whether it is true.

ambiguities: Odette's charge against oncle Adolphe is unverified and follows immediately on advice he gave against her interest, so his diminishment is recorded as a staged accusation rather than an established fact.

Swann's worldly eminence is real but is offered as consolation, compared to an invalid reading a banquet menu; the elevation and the abasement are both fully present rather than cancelling each other.
